## Why This Is Asked
Evaluates plugin architecture, isolation, and runtime extensibility in CLI tooling.

## Key Concepts
- Command pattern in plugins
- Runtime registry with versioning
- Sandboxed loading and security
- Hot reload and fallback semantics

## Code Example
```javascript
export interface Command {
  name: string;
  description: string;
  execute(args: string[]): Promise<number>;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle dependency conflicts and plugin sandboxing security concerns?
- What metrics would you collect to monitor plugin health and performance?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests knowledge of the Command pattern, runtime extensibility, and execution isolation in CLI tools. It also probes safe dynamic loading and simple governance for enabling/disabling commands.

## Key Concepts
- Command pattern and runtime registry
- Isolation per run and optional hooks
- Dynamic plugin-style extension without rebuilds

## Code Example
```javascript
// Minimal sketch
interface Command { name: string; description?: string; exec: (args: string[], ctx: any) => void | Promise<void> }
class Registry { register(n: string, c: Command){ /* store */ } resolve(n:string): Command|undefined{ } list(): string[] { } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle name conflicts or versioned commands?
- How would you test commands with mocks for ctx?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to design runtime extensibility with minimal core changes, using a Registry and Factory-like pattern alongside a clean Backend abstraction.

## Key Concepts
- Registry pattern for dynamic extension
- Strategy-like renderers decoupled from backends
- Backend adapters for SVG and Canvas

## Code Example
```javascript
interface Backend { begin(): void; draw(path: string): void; fill(): void; }
interface Renderer { render(shape: Shape, backend: Backend): void; }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test adding a new renderer without rendering a full scene?
- How would you handle renderer lifecycle (initialization, disposal) in a long-running app?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Real-world fault tolerance requires dynamic policy changes without redeploys. This tests design extensibility, runtime registries, and per-endpoint isolation.

## Key Concepts
- Runtime extensibility and registries
- Pipeline/Chain of Responsibility pattern
- Per-endpoint isolation and non-blocking evaluation
- Metrics and safe error handling

## Code Example
```javascript
interface IPolicy { name: string; configure(params: any): void; onCall(ctx: any, next: () => Promise<any>): Promise<any> }
interface IPolicyFactory { create(config?: any): IPolicy }
class PolicyRegistry { private map = new Map<string, IPolicyFactory>(); register(name: string, f: IPolicyFactory): void; create(name: string, config?: any): IPolicy }
class PolicyPipeline { constructor(policies: IPolicy[]); async execute(ctx: any, fn: ()=> Promise<any>): Promise<any> }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test policy interactions across distributed instances?
- How would you handle policy versioning and backward compatibility?

## Why This Is Asked
This question probes understanding of runtime extensibility using a registry to plug in new validators without altering core logic.

- Registry pattern for dynamic type lookup
- Strategy/Chain approach for composed validation
- TypeScript interfaces and factories
- Extensibility vs. rigidity

```javascript
export type ValidationResult = { ok: boolean; errors?: string[] }
```

- How to handle async validators?
- How to aggregate multiple validation errors?
